lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- The Doctorate, in English
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Aguinaldo Ballon | Lesson 6 -- The Doctorate, in English

listenings.text: Welcome to the seminar on infrastructure regulation. Some of you come from Brazil, some from Italy and some from Spain, so English is the language that we all share. Please don't worry about your accent. What I care about is precision. Every week, one student presents a case study which he or she has chosen. The presentation is short, fifteen minutes, and it must start with a clear definition of the problem. After that, the group discusses it. The students who participate most are not the ones with perfect English. They are the ones who come prepared, with a question.

I did the international part of my doctorate at a university in Madrid, where most of the classes were in English. The first month was difficult. I understood the texts, which I could read slowly at home, but I did not understand the discussions, which were very fast. My supervisor, who was very patient, gave me a simple tip. Before every class, read the abstract of each article twice, and write one question. It worked. After two months, I was the student who asked the first question in every class. My thesis, which I defended last year, is about precedent in energy regulation.

an earlier decision used as an example for later cases
a detailed study of one real example
a short summary at the beginning of an academic article
a long piece of original research written for a university degree
legal responsibility, especially for paying for damage or loss

reading.rtitle: Who Pays When a Concession Fails?
paras: Abstract. This article studies the question of liability in infrastructure concessions which end before the contract term. When a concession fails, the state, the private company and the lenders often disagree about who has to pay for the losses. Most of the existing literature review focuses on the contract itself, and less attention is given to the role of the regulator, which is the agency that controls the sector during the whole contract.

The article uses a case study of twelve highway concessions in Brazil and Chile, where different legal traditions produced different results. In Chile, where the framework is older, the courts followed a clear precedent. In Brazil, the decisions changed from case to case, and the same clause was interpreted in different ways by different judges.

The author, who has advised both governments and investors, argues that stable regulation is more important than detailed contracts. The article concludes that a regulator whose decisions are predictable reduces the cost of capital, and it suggests three changes for future contracts. It is part of a larger doctoral thesis, which will be published next year.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B1 reading, written for this lesson in the format of an academic abstract
